Larissa New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Larisa, Greece

Not demolished. Jews first settled in Larissa in the 5th century, forming a small Romaniot community that flourished under Ottoman rule from the late 14th century; a Sephardi congregation also existed by the 16th-17th centuries, with emissaries from Eretz Israel involved in settling community disputes over the following two centuries. Population reached 1,500 (of 6,000 total) by 1848; an 1857 fire destroyed two synagogues, leaving 250 families destitute. The Alliance Israelite ran a school from 1868-1874 alongside existing religious education; population peaked around 2,000 by 1880 before falling to 1,069 by 1907. Early 20th-century Zionist organizations and cultural movements flourished; by the 1920s, seven synagogues served a community of 1,175 (as of 1940). Spring 1941 bombing and an earthquake forced most residents to flee to nearby villages; in March 1944, 235 remaining Jews were arrested by Germans, with 225 deported to Auschwitz - only six survived. Postwar recovery made Larissa one of Greece's largest Jewish communities after Athens and Salonika. This cemetery's founding is unknown, presumed 17th-19th century, and remains active, apparently having absorbed reburials from an older cemetery.
